q7.answer: The raw token is generated in step A, hashed for storage, and put into the link inside the "reset" email job that the API enqueues after the commit. The email worker sends that job, so the raw token exists only in the queued payload and the email.

q8.answer: The server computes sha256 of the token in the URL and looks it up by the indexed token_hash column. The link is good only if a row exists with consumed_at IS NULL and expires_at > now(). Otherwise (no row, expired, used or superseded) the user sees the "expired, request a new one" page. The page load does not consume the link.

q9.answer: The count is not stored separately. It is computed from the password_reset_tokens rows, as the number of that account's rows with created_at in the last hour. Old requests drop out simply because they age past the one-hour window. Rows are kept at least an hour, and cleanup may delete rows older than a day.

q10.answer: In step A, inside the same transaction and under the row lock on the user, all of the account's earlier rows with consumed_at IS NULL are marked consumed (superseded) just before the new row is inserted. This happens only when the request is under the limit. The update and insert commit together, before the email is enqueued.

q11.answer: In one transaction, the link is burned (consumed_at set), users.password_hash is updated, and all of the user's sessions rows are deleted. They commit together or not at all. The "password changed" email is enqueued only after that commit, and if the enqueue fails it is logged and the reset is not undone.

q12.answer: The submit runs a conditional UPDATE ... SET consumed_at=now() WHERE token_hash=h AND consumed_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now() RETURNING user_id inside the transaction. Postgres lets only one of the concurrent statements win. The loser gets 0 rows, rolls back and sees the expired page. Only the winner changes the password.
